import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 244

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/244](https://www.erdosproblems.com/244)
-/

namespace Erdos244

/-- Let $C > 1$. Does the set of integers of the form $p + \lfloor C^k \rfloor$,
for some prime $p$ and $k\geq 0$, have density $>0$? -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_244 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ C > (1 : ℝ), 0 < { p + ⌊C ^ k⌋₊ | (p) (k) (_ : p.Prime) }.lowerDensity := by
  sorry

/-- Romanoff [Ro34] proved that the answer is yes if $C$ is an integer.

[Ro34] Romanoff, N. P., _Über einige Sätze der additiven Zahlentheorie_.
Math. Ann. (1934), 668-678. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_244.variants.Romanoff {C : ℕ} (hC : 1 < C) :
    0 < { p + ⌊C ^ k⌋₊ | (p) (k) (_ : p.Prime) }.lowerDensity := by
  sorry

end Erdos244

reformulations.difference: Lean uses natural-number-valued floor and the library's lower-density convention counting [0,N), whereas the conventional formulation uses integer floor and counts in [1,N].
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For C>1 and k∈ℕ, C^k≥1, so Nat.floor agrees with integer floor after casting. Every represented number is at least 3. Consequently the counts in [0,N) and [1,N] differ by at most one, and their ratios differ by at most 1/N, giving identical liminfs. Ding explicitly identifies the question as asking for positive lower asymptotic density, not existence of a positive natural-density limit. The floor identities and positive-lower-density characterization were proved in the scratch file; the endpoint comparison was checked mathematically.

sources_consulted: Yuchen Ding, On two Romanoff type problems of Erdős, arXiv:2503.22700v4, abstract, introduction, Theorem 1.1 and notation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22700; LaTeX source: https://arxiv.org/e-print/2503.22700
N. P. Romanoff, Über einige Sätze der additiven Zahlentheorie, Math. Ann. 109 (1934), 668–678. Publisher preview, including the footnote defining positive density: https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01449161
review.notes: Both declarations were checked and match the sources. The general problem remains open; Romanoff's integer-base case is correctly marked solved. Successful Lean experiments in /workspace/review/checks.lean verify the inferred natural-number generators, primality requirement, floor semantics, smallest represented number, integer specialization, finite counting intervals, and bounded density ratios. Thus neither infinite-set cardinality defaults nor division at N=0 changes either statement.
